segments: The summer I turned twelve, my parents sent me to spend July with my great-aunt Hedda in Callow Bend, a river town with two churches, one traffic light, and a hardware store that also sold bait. I had met Hedda only twice, both times at funerals, and I expected a month of silence and boiled vegetables. She had retired the spring before.
Her house was narrow and dim, with a porch that sagged toward the road.
On the first evening I noticed a framed photograph on the mantel, the only picture in the room, and Hedda caught me looking at it.
Callow Bend sits where the river turns hard to the east, and the water there runs deep and fast. A ferry had once crossed at the bend, but it had stopped running before I was born.
